vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: openclaw360
Version: 0.1.9

The openclaw360 skill is a comprehensive security utility designed to protect AI agents through prompt injection detection, tool call authorization, and static analysis of other skills. It follows security best practices by operating entirely locally, using Ed25519 signatures for log and backup integrity, and explicitly disabling automatic model invocation via the 'disable-model-invocation' flag. The installation process uses a pinned GitHub commit (5fd69db) to ensure code consistency, and the instructions provide a structured framework for the agent to act as a security gatekeeper without any evidence of data exfiltration, persistence mechanisms, or malicious intent.

llm.summary: The skill is plausibly what it claims (a local CLI-based security helper) but has small inconsistencies and runtime assumptions that deserve review before installation.

dimensions.detail: Name/description align with required items: it needs python3 and stores data under ~/.openclaw360, which fits a local CLI security tool. Minor mismatch: the SKILL.md scan default path is listed as ~/.openclaw/skills (missing '360'), which may be a typo or point to a different platform directory—this should be clarified.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: The SKILL.md instructs the agent to run the openclaw360 CLI on every input/tool/output (proactive checks). This is logical for a runtime security helper, but conflicts with the metadata flag disable-model-invocation: true (which prevents the skill from being invoked automatically by the model). The instructions also specify a permissive downgrade policy (if checks fail, continue execution), which weakens protections and should be a conscious tradeoff.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: No automated install spec in registry, but SKILL.md contains pip install commands that pull from a GitHub repo at a pinned commit hash. Using a pinned commit is good practice, but installing code directly from a GitHub URL carries the usual risk of executing third-party code — the SKILL.md states the user runs these commands manually rather than the platform auto-installing them.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: No environment variables or external credentials are requested. The only config requirements are under ~/.openclaw360/ including an identity key (Ed25519) used for local signing — this is proportionate to claimed backup/audit features. Verify you are comfortable with a local key being created (file permissions should be 0600 as claimed).
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: always:false and disable-model-invocation:true limit persistent/automatic invocation — reasonable for a user-invocable security tool. The skill writes only to ~/.openclaw360/ per its docs. Note: the instructions expect the agent to run CLI checks proactively; whether the platform permits that behavior depends on runtime policies.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: This skill appears to be a local CLI-based runtime security helper and mostly consistent with that purpose, but review these before installing: 1) Inspect the referenced GitHub repo and the pinned commit hash before running pip install (installing from GitHub executes third‑party code). 2) Confirm the default scan path (~/.openclaw/skills) is intentional and not a typo—the skill may scan other skill directories. 3) Understand the downgrade behavior: if the tool fails it will instruct the agent to continue anyway, which weakens protection. 4) Ensure you're comfortable with a local Ed25519 key and audit logs stored under ~/.openclaw360/ (confirm file permissions). 5) Verify your agent runtime actually allows invoking local CLI commands as the SKILL.md expects; if the platform doesn't permit that, the described proactive checks won't run. If any of these are unacceptable, run the tool in an isolated environment or review the source before use.
